## Participants

A total of 616 participants were recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk). MTurk allows researchers to collect high-quality data rapidly among demographically diverse individuals \cite{buhrmesterAmazonMechanicalTurk2011}. Prior work has shown that MTurk can be reliably used to make inferences about a number of broader populations of interest \cite{coppockGeneralizingSurveyExperiments2019, huffWhoAreThese2015, johnsonAmazonMechanicalTurk2020}. The participants were required to be located within the United States, over the age of 18, fluent in English. While limitations apply the MTurk studies (see Limitations in the Discussion), studies have shown that the quality of MTurk responses can improve with \textit{a priori} researcher constraints \cite{peerReputationSufficientCondition2014, cheungAmazonMechanicalTurk2017, thomasValidityMechanicalTurk2017}. In the current study, we required that participants had previously completed at least 100 tasks and maintained at least a 95\% approval rating on MTurk. We additionally applied exclusions to further ensure that we analyzed high-quality behavioral data (see Exclusions). Our final sample was `r sample`participants.The total sample consisted of `r n.female` females, $M_{age}$ = `r mage` years of age ($SD_{age}$ = `r sdage`), with `r n.HighSchool` high school, `r n.Undergraduate` undergraduate, and `r n.Postgraduate` postgraduate, and identified as White/Caucasian (*n* = `r n.white`), Asian (*n* = `r n.asian`), Hispanic/Latino (*n* = `r n.hispanic`), Black/African American (*n* = `r n.black`), Pacific Islander (*n* = `r n.pacific`) other/multiple (*n* = `r n.othereth`), or did not disclose their ethnicity (*n* = `r n.notreported`). The included subjects completed the task in an average of $M_{task}$ = `r mtask` minutes ($SD_{task}$ = `r sdtask`) and the survey in an average of $M_{survey}$ = `r msurvey` minutes ($SD_{survey}$ = `r sdsurvey`).

## Exlclusion Criteria

In line with recommendations for studies conducted using Amazons Mechanical Turk (AMT) service, careful instructions and \textit{a priori} exclusion criteria were applied to further ensure data quality \cite{crumpEvaluatingAmazonMechanical2013}. Using a multi-method approach to detect careless/invalid responses in online samples, several data exclusion criteria were applied \cite{curranMethodsDetectionCarelessly2016}. A total of `r excluded` participants were excluded. Participants single trials were excluded if response times were either 250 milli-seconds or above 90 seconds. Given that participants had ample time to respond to each question (up to as long until they made a decision), we reasoned that these participants were not devoting sufficient attention to the task. Additionally, having considered trial wise exclusions, participants were also excluded for failure to complete at least 40 trials in the specified range. Finally, participants were excluded for failure of passing four attention check items and a total survey completion time below five minutes. Because our survey battery involved 11 different assessments, we reasoned that a total completion time below five minutes reflected a careless responder. Our overall exclusion rate of `r exlclusion_rate`\% is well in line with research findings studying quality control measures on MTurk \cite{crumpEvaluatingAmazonMechanical2013, downsAreYourParticipants2010, paolacciTurkUnderstandingMechanical2014}.

*Data analytic exclusions*
We decided in advance chose to exclude the 5\% of participants with the poorest model fit based on Nagelkerke’s $R^2$ (see also \cite{walasekHowMakeLoss20141208, walasekContextdependentSensitivityLosses20181025}, with the objective of removing participants who responded most randomly and inconsistently. Lastly, participants were excluded for selecting a “yes” or “no” response at least 90\% of the total number of trials. These patterns of stereotyped responses preclude the ability to estimate reliable coefficients in our statistical models. Furthermore, they could result from individuals who are not responding to the information presented on screen during the task. None of the analyses reported yields qualitatively different results if all participants’ data are retained.

The average trial completion time was $M_{trial}$ = `r mtrial` ($SD_{trial}$ = `r sdtrial`). Participants were mostly unwilling to choose a treatment. Overall, the average rejection probability across subjects was $M_{No}$ = `r mno` ($SD_{No}$ = `r sdno`), with 73\% of participants being more likely to select no treatment than a treatment. 


##Risk, benefit marginal effects for each cog domain
```{r echo=FALSE, dpi= 300}
data.h %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, condition, marginal.effect.risk, marginal.effect.gain) %>% 
  reshape2::melt(id = c("user_id", "condition") , variable.name = "type", value.name = "marginal.effect") -> test

ggplot(test, aes(condition, marginal.effect, fill = condition))+
  geom_half_violin(side = "r") +
  geom_half_point(side = "l", alpha=0.5, transformation = position_jitter(width = .15))+
  coord_flip()+
  theme_minimal()+
   labs(title = "Average Marginal Effect by Cognitive Domain",
       subtitle = "",
       x = "Cognitive Domain", 
       y = "Marginal Effect",
       color = "")+theme(legend.position = "none")+
       facet_wrap(~ type, scale = "free_y", nrow = 2)

plotdata <- test %>%
  group_by(type, condition) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            median = median(marginal.effect),
            mean = mean(marginal.effect),
            sd = sd(marginal.effect),
            se = sd/sqrt(n),
            ci = qt(0.975, df = n - 1) * sd / sqrt(n)) %>% na.omit()

knitr::kable(plotdata[1:7,], caption = "Descriptives for Risk by Cog domain")%>%  
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
knitr::kable(plotdata[8:14,], caption = "Descriptives for Gain by Cog domain")%>%  
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")

data.h %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, marginal.effect.gain) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(marginal.effect.gain))+ 
  geom_histogram(fill = "deepskyblue",
                 color="black",
                 bins = 60)+theme_bw()
data.h %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, marginal.effect.risk) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(marginal.effect.risk))+ 
  geom_histogram(fill = "indianred3",
                 color="black",
                 bins = 60)+theme_bw()

data.h %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, marginal.effect.risk, marginal.effect.gain) %>% 
  mutate(marginal.effect.risk = marginal.effect.risk) %>% 
  melt(id = c("user_id"), variable.name = "type", value.name = "marginal.effect") %>% 
  ggplot(aes(marginal.effect, fill=type)) + geom_histogram(color="black",bins = 60, alpha = .8)+theme_bw()+
  theme(legend.position="none") +
  facet_wrap(~ type, scale = "free_y", nrow = 2) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype="dashed", size=1.5)
```

**##Statistical test for risk vs. benefit**
```{r testing for risk & benefit difference}
data.h %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, condition, marginal.effect.risk, marginal.effect.gain, Yes, No) %>% 
  mutate(marginal.effect.risk = log(abs(marginal.effect.risk+1))) %>% 
  mutate(marginal.effect.gain = log(abs(marginal.effect.gain+1))) %>% 
 #mutate(marginal.effect.risk = -1 * marginal.effect.risk) %>% 
  reshape2::melt(id = c("user_id", "condition", "Yes", "No") , variable.name = "type", value.name = "marginal.effect") -> test 

#note that the results do not change when I remove the outlier

test$user_id <- factor(test$user_id)

t <- t.test(marginal.effect ~ type,  paired = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95,var.equal = F, data =test)
tab <- map_df(list(t), tidy)
knitr::kable(tab[c("estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "parameter", "conf.low", 
"conf.high", "method")], caption = "Parired T-test")%>%  
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
# plot
ggstatsplot::ggwithinstats(
  data = test,
  x = type,
  y = marginal.effect,
  title = "Paired T-test of log transformed absolute value of the marginal effects",
  subtitle = "log transformed absolute value of the marginal effects",
  caption = "",
  ggstatsplot.layer = FALSE,
  point.path = F,
  mean.plotting = F
)

test %>% 
  group_by(type) %>% 
  summarise(
    median = median(marginal.effect),
    mean = mean(marginal.effect),
    sd = sd(marginal.effect)
  )
#effectsize::t_to_d(-2.4246,423, paired = T)
```
The Paired t-test suggests that the difference of marginal.effect between gains and losses (mean of the differences =  -0.000719878) is significant (difference = , 95% CI [-0.0013034596, -0.0001362965], t(424) = -2.425, p < .05) and can be considered as small (Hedge's g = -0.12).

Results thus indicate a slight but significant preference for gains (M = 0.003030959, SD = 0.004875783) over losses (M = 0.002311081, SD = 0.004647267).

**##Interdomain stability**
```{r cog domain h2, echo=FALSE}
aov.1 <- stats::oneway.test(log(abs(marginal.effect.risk+1)) ~ condition, data = data.h, var.equal= F)
aov.2 <- stats::oneway.test(log(abs(marginal.effect.gain+1))~ condition, data = data.h, var.equal= F)

# plot
ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats(data = data.h,
  x = condition,
  y = marginal.effect.risk,
  title = "Distribution of average marginal effects for risks across cognitive domain"
)+theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

# plot
ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats(
  data = data.h,
  x = condition,
  y = marginal.effect.gain,
  title = "Distribution of average marginal effects for gains across cognitive domain"
)+ theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
#create a table 
tab <- map_df(list(aov.1,aov.2), tidy)
knitr::kable(tab[c("num.df", "den.df", "statistic", "p.value", "method")], caption = "one way anova testing cognitve domain; (Risk and Gain)")%>%  
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
```
An analysis of variance showed that the effect of cognitive domain for losses was not significant, F(6, 371) = 0.36, p = 0.902 and can be considered as very small (partial omega squared = -0.01).

An analysis of variance showed that the effect of cognitive domain for gains was not significant, F(6, 371) = 0.85, p = 0.529 and can be considered as very small (partial omega squared = -0.01).

**##Do people use nonlinear weighting of probabilities?**
```{r cor h3 analysis}
Neuroethics_Judgement %>% 
  group_by(user_id) %>% 
  mutate(pearson.corr = cor(risk, gain, method = "pearson")) %>% 
  ungroup(user_id) %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, condition, risk, gain, experimental_treatment_selected, Yes, No, pearson.corr) %>% 
   mutate(experimental_treatment_selected = ifelse(experimental_treatment_selected == "Yes to treatment", 1, 0)) -> test

continuous <- c("risk", "gain", "pearson.corr")

test[,continuous] <- scale(test[,continuous])  
#model 1 only linear terms
#cl <- makePSOCKcluster() #use parallel processing

registerDoParallel() #use parallel processing
#start with risk, and gain
m.1 <- glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + risk + gain  +
               (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
             data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
             control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
             nAGQ = 0)

#add poly gain
m.2 <- glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + risk + gain + I(gain^2) +
               (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
             data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
             control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
             nAGQ = 0)
#just add poly risk 
m.3 <- glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2) + 
               (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
             data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
             control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
             nAGQ = 0)
#linear interaction
m.4 <-  glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + 
                risk + gain + 
                I(gain^2) + I(risk^2) + 
                risk:gain + 
                (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
              data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
              control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
              nAGQ = 0)
#add risk gain^2 interaction
m.5 <-  glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + 
                risk + gain +
                I(risk^2) + I(gain^2)+
                risk:gain+
                risk:I(gain^2) +
                (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
              data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
              control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
              nAGQ = 0)
#add gain risk^2 interaction
m.6 <-  glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + 
                risk + gain +
                I(risk^2) + I(gain^2)+
                risk:gain+
                risk:I(gain^2) +
                gain:I(risk^2) + 
                (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
              data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
              control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
              nAGQ = 0)
#add last interaction
m.7 <-  glmer(experimental_treatment_selected ~ pearson.corr + 
                risk + gain +
                I(risk^2) + I(gain^2)+
                risk:gain+
                risk:I(gain^2) +
                gain:I(risk^2) + 
                I(risk^2):I(gain^2)+
                (risk + gain + I(gain^2) + I(risk^2)| user_id), 
              data = test, family = binomial(link="logit"), 
              control=glmerControl(optimizer="bobyqa"),
              nAGQ = 0)

table <-anova(m.1, m.2, m.3, m.4, m.5, m.6, m.7, type = "LRT")
tab <- map_df(list(table), tidy)
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
knitr::kable(tab[c("term", "npar", "AIC", "BIC", "logLik", "deviance", "statistic", 
                   "df", "p.value")], caption = "Model Comparison")%>%  
  kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position")
##
#Anova(m.6, type = "III")
ggeffects::ggpredict(m.6, terms=c("risk [all]", "gain [all]"))
ggeffects::ggpredict(m.6, terms=c("gain [all]", "risk"))

stopImplicitCluster()
```

#Individual Differences

Note I have run these without the outliers and with; no difference. 
##**Age**

```{r age data, echo=FALSE}
data.h %>% 
  mutate(marginal.effect.risk = log(abs(marginal.effect.risk + 1))) %>% 
  mutate(marginal.effect.gain = log(abs(marginal.effect.gain + 1))) %>% 
  mutate(YN_diff = Yes - No, user_id = factor(user_id), age = 1/age) %>% 
  dplyr::select(marginal.effect.risk, marginal.effect.gain, age, YN_diff) %>%
  na.omit() -> data.age
```

```{r education plotting}
education <- data.education %>%
  group_by(education) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
```

#suppTable S3 

Generalized linear modeling results using the "lme4" package (R
version x.X.X; “lme4” version X.X-XX).

For each state the model formula, results and fixed effect terms: 
```{r supp}

get_model_stuff <- function(model){
  stuff <- list() 
  x <- summary(model)
  formula = x[["call"]]
  stuff[[1]] = toString(formula)
  results = broom.mixed::glance(model) %>% select(AIC, BIC, logLik, deviance, df.residual)
  stuff[[2]] = results
  terms   = broom.mixed::tidy(model) %>% filter(effect == "fixed") %>% 
  select(term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value)
  stuff[[3]] = terms
  return(stuff)
}
models <- c(m.1, m.2, m.3, m.4, m.5, m.6, m.7)

models %>% 
map(get_model_stuff) -> supp
kable(supp) #we are on to something here! 
```
